walkthroughs.body_html:
Paper 1: Fiction and Imaginative Writing — a core area of GCSE English Language.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Paper 1: Fiction and Imaginative Writing brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Paper 1: Fiction and Imaginative Writing.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is a speech act according to Searle/Austin?
options: A speech act is any time someone speaks.
Text types are arbitrary and have no patterns.
A speech act is a performance or a play.
An utterance that performs an action — promising, ordering, apologising, declaring. Speech acts have locutionary (what's said), illocutionary (intended force) and perlocutionary (effect) dimensions.

mcqs.q: Why do text types have predictable features?
options: Register is the same as accent.
Text types have fixed features just because tradition says so.
Text types are arbitrary and have no patterns.
Conventions develop because they serve communicative purpose — a recipe needs imperatives because it instructs; a news report needs the inverted pyramid because of how readers scan.
Register is just how loud you speak.
Register is the same as accent.
A variety of language used in a particular social setting — varying by formality, field (topic) and mode (spoken/written) to suit audience and purpose.
A speech act is a performance or a play.
